## Dexamethasone: Regulatory Safety History

### ✅ Overall Conclusion: Dexamethasone Has NOT Been Withdrawn from the Market for Safety Reasons

Dexamethasone, as a drug class, has **never been withdrawn from any market for safety or effectiveness reasons**. The FDA has repeatedly and explicitly confirmed this across numerous specific formulations. However, there are important nuances involving specific formulations and a significant safety warning issued for its injectable form. Here is the full breakdown:

---

### 1. 📋 Multiple FDA Determinations: NOT Withdrawn for Safety

The FDA has formally investigated several discontinued dexamethasone formulations and, in every case, determined they were **not** withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons. These formulations were discontinued for commercial/business reasons only.

- **DECADRON-LA (Dexamethasone Acetate Injection, 8 mg/mL):** 
After considering the citizen petition and reviewing its records, FDA determined that DECADRON-LA (dexamethasone acetate injection), 8 mg/mL, was not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
 
In a letter to the agency dated June 25, 2002, Merck requested that NDA 16-675 be withdrawn because the drug is no longer marketed, and Merck noted that the NDA was not withdrawn because of safety reasons.

  - 📎 Source: [Federal Register, August 24, 2004](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2004/08/24/04-19287/determination-that-decadron-la-dexamethasone-acetate-injection-was-not-withdrawn-from-sale-for)

- **DECADRON (Dexamethasone) Tablets, 1.5 mg:** 
The agency determined that Merck's DECADRON (dexamethasone) tablets, 1.5 mg, were not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. FDA reviewed its files for records concerning the withdrawal of DECADRON tablets, 1.5 mg, from sale. There is no indication that the decision not to market them commercially is a function of safety or effectiveness concerns.
 
According to Merck's 1997 annual report, the 1.5-mg dose strength, among others, of DECADRON tablets was discontinued in 1997.

  - 📎 Source: [Federal Register, December 28, 2005](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2005/12/28/E5-7875/determination-that-decadron-dexamethasone-tablets-15-milligrams-were-not-withdrawn-from-sale-for)

- **DECADRON (Dexamethasone Sodium Phosphate) Solution/Drops, 0.1%:** 
The FDA has determined that DECADRON (dexamethasone sodium phosphate) solution/drops, equivalent to 0.1 percent phosphate, was not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
 
The FDA independently evaluated relevant literature and data for possible postmarketing adverse events and found no information that would indicate that this drug product was withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.

  - 📎 Source: [Federal Register, April 9, 2025](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/09/2025-06046/determination-that-decadron-dexamethasone-sodium-phosphate-solutiondrops-equivalent-to-01-percent)

- **DEXAMETHASONE Elixir, 0.5 mg/5 mL:** 
The FDA has determined that DEXAMETHASONE (dexamethasone) elixir, 0.5 mg/5 mL, was not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
 
In a letter dated November 16, 2021, Wockhardt Bio AG notified FDA that the elixir was being discontinued, and FDA moved the drug product to the "Discontinued Drug Product List" section of the Orange Book.

  - 📎 Source: [Federal Register, May 6, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/06/2026-08939/determination-that-dexamethasone-dexamethasone-elixir-05-milligrams5-milliliters-was-not-withdrawn)

- **DECASPRAY (Dexamethasone) Topical Aerosol, 0.04% and AEROSEB-DEX 0.01%:** 
The FDA determined that DECASPRAY (dexamethasone) Topical Aerosol, 0.04%, and AEROSEB-DEX (dexamethasone) Topical Aerosol, 0.01%, were not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.

  - 📎 Source: [Federal Register, February 9, 2011](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2011/02/09/2011-2890/determination-that-decaspray-dexamethasone-topical-aerosol-004-and-aeroseb-dex-dexamethasone-topical)

---

### 2. 🚨 Dexamethasone Nasal Spray: Withdrawn from the U.S. Market (1998)

One notable case involves the nasal spray formulation. 
Dexamethasone nasal was withdrawn from the U.S. market in 1998.
 The reason cited in the literature is largely associated with systemic absorption concerns (including Cushing's syndrome with prolonged use), though the FDA's formal determination was that this withdrawal was not formally classified as a safety-based removal in the regulatory sense. The drug is not on the FDA's official list of drugs withdrawn for safety reasons (21 CFR 216.24).
  - 📎 Source: [Drugs.com – Dexamethasone Nasal](https://www.drugs.com/mtm/dexamethasone-nasal.html)

---

### 3. ⚠️ FDA Safety Warning (Not a Black Box Warning) for Epidural Corticosteroid Injections — Includes Dexamethasone (2014)

This is the most significant safety-related regulatory action involving dexamethasone. In April 2014, the FDA issued a **Drug Safety Communication** requiring label changes for all injectable corticosteroids, including dexamethasone.


In April 2014, the U.S. FDA issued a drug safety communication entitled "FDA requires label changes to warn of rare but serious neurologic problems after epidural corticosteroid injections (ESI) for pain."



The FDA warned that injection of corticosteroids into the epidural space of the spine may result in rare but serious adverse events, including loss of vision, stroke, paralysis, and death.



Injectable corticosteroids covered by this warning include methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone, triamcinolone, betamethasone, and dexamethasone. Corticosteroids are not approved by the FDA for injection into the epidural space.



In 2009, the FDA began evaluating serious neurologic events associated with epidural glucocorticoid injections. Between 1997 and 2014, a total of 90 serious and sometimes fatal neurologic events were reported to the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), including cases of paraplegia, quadriplegia, spinal cord infarction, and stroke.

Here’s a target-focused answer that separates **multiple myeloma biology** from **the clinically known glucocorticoid mechanism of dexamethasone**.

## 1. Disease mechanism

**Core pathophysiological defect in multiple myeloma (MM):**  
MM is a **clonal malignancy of plasma cells** in the bone marrow. Its core defect is not a single NR3C1-driven lesion, but the **pathologic expansion/survival of malignant plasma cells** caused by primary genetic events such as **Ig translocations or hyperdiploidy**, followed by secondary oncogenic alterations and strong support from the **bone marrow microenvironment**. This produces persistent plasma-cell survival, proliferation, and resistance to apoptosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8743906/?utm_source=openai))

**Is NR3C1 deficient or overactive in MM?**  
For MM **as a disease**, the primary molecular defect is **not established as NR3C1 overactivity**. If anything, the literature most consistently links **reduced or impaired NR3C1/glucocorticoid receptor (GR) function** with **glucocorticoid resistance**, not with disease initiation as the central driver. Studies in MM show that **GR/NR3C1 expression is an important limiting factor** for dexamethasone-induced cell death, and resistant disease can involve **NR3C1 downregulation, mutation, or functional impairment**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))

**Bottom line for Q1:**  
- **Core MM defect:** malignant plasma-cell survival/proliferation driven by oncogenic genomic lesions plus marrow microenvironmental support. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8743906/?utm_source=openai))  
- **NR3C1 status:** **not a primary overactive driver of MM**; available evidence more strongly supports that **loss/reduction of NR3C1 activity contributes to steroid resistance** in at least a subset of MM. So, if forced into the binary you gave, **NR3C1 is closer to “deficient” than “overactive,” but this is not the core disease-initiating defect.** ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))

## 2. Target-specific direction

You asked to use the premise that, **for NR3C1 specifically**, dexamethasone should be treated as an **inhibitor** because of IC50/Ki binding activity in ChEMBL, and to **ignore** its annotated agonist mechanism on another target/mechanism context.

Under that framing:

- In MM, the evidence does **not** indicate that NR3C1 is pathologically overactive and needing inhibition.  
- Instead, NR3C1/GR function is generally required for the canonical anti-myeloma glucocorticoid response, and **reduced NR3C1 function is associated with resistance** to dexamethasone-induced apoptosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))

Therefore, if dexamethasone’s **direct effect on NR3C1 itself** were truly **inhibitory**, that action would **not correct** the MM-associated defect. It would more likely **worsen or at least oppose** the direction associated with glucocorticoid sensitivity, because suppressing NR3C1 would be expected to move cells further toward the **low-GR / GR-impaired** state associated with steroid resistance. This is an inference from the disease/response biology, not a direct clinical observation of “NR3C1 inhibition therapy” in MM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))

**Bottom line for Q2:**  
**WORSEN**, or at minimum **fail to compensate for**, the relevant NR3C1-related biology in MM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))

## 3. Clinical use anchor

**Yes. Dexamethasone is an established treatment component in MM.**  
FDA labeling for **HEMADY (dexamethasone)** states it is indicated **in combination with other anti-myeloma products for adults with multiple myeloma**. FDA approval materials also note that dexamethasone has long been a backbone component of MM regimens and is included in multiple approved combinations. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2019/211379s000lbl.pdf))

**Confirmed clinical mechanism through NR3C1:**  
The confirmed anti-myeloma mechanism is through the **glucocorticoid receptor (GR), encoded by NR3C1)**, where dexamethasone **binds/activates GR** and promotes **anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic transcriptional programs** in myeloma cells. FDA’s clinical review explicitly states that dexamethasone’s anti-myeloma effect is **mediated via the glucocorticoid receptor**. Experimental MM literature further shows that GR expression is required for dexamethasone-induced apoptosis and that downstream mediators include **GILZ** and **BIM**. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211379Orig1s000MedR.pdf))

**Disease caused by NR3C1 dysfunction?**  
I did not find an approved therapy whose rationale is to **treat a disease caused by NR3C1 loss by inhibiting NR3C1**. The clinically validated relationship runs the other way here: **functional NR3C1 is needed for dexamethasone efficacy in MM**, and impaired NR3C1 contributes to resistance. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211379Orig1s000MedR.pdf))

## Overall conclusion

1. **MM’s main defect** is **malignant plasma-cell expansion/survival** driven by genomic lesions and marrow support, **not NR3C1 overactivation**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8743906/?utm_source=openai))  
2. Relative to the NR3C1 axis, MM is more consistent with **reduced/impaired NR3C1 function in resistant states** than with excessive NR3C1 activity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))  
3. Therefore, if you force dexamethasone’s **direct NR3C1 action** to be interpreted as **inhibitory**, that would be predicted to **worsen**, not correct, the relevant NR3C1-related disease biology. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4694963/))  
4. Clinically, however, dexamethasone is indeed used in MM, and the **validated mechanism is the opposite direction**: **GR/NR3C1-mediated glucocorticoid receptor activation leading to myeloma-cell apoptosis**. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2019/211379s000lbl.pdf))

## Prednisolone: Withdrawals, Black Box Warnings, and Safety Recalls

### 1. ✅ NOT Withdrawn from Market for Safety or Effectiveness Reasons

The most authoritative and recent regulatory determination on this topic comes directly from the U.S. FDA:


The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has determined that prednisolone tablet, 5 milligrams (mg), was **not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness**.



In a letter dated April 28, 1992, Heather Drug Co. Inc. notified FDA that prednisolone tablet, 5 mg, was being discontinued. FDA then moved the drug product to the "Discontinued Drug Product List" section of the Orange Book.


However, this discontinuation was **not** for safety reasons. 
The FDA will continue to list prednisolone tablet, 5 mg, in the "Discontinued Drug Product List" section of the Orange Book, which delineates drug products that have been discontinued from marketing for **reasons other than safety or effectiveness**.



After considering a citizen petition and reviewing Agency records, FDA determined under § 314.161 that prednisolone tablet, 5 mg, was not withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness. The petitioner identified no data or other information suggesting that prednisolone tablet, 5 mg, was withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness.


📄 **Source:** [Federal Register – June 26, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/26/2026-12959/determination-that-prednisolone-tablet-5-milligrams-was-not-withdrawn-from-sale-for-reasons-of)

---

### 2. ❌ No FDA Black Box Warning for Prednisolone


There is **no formal FDA Black Box Warning** for prednisolone (or its prodrug prednisone), but severe warnings relate to adrenal suppression and infection risk.


The FDA's prescribing information for prednisolone-containing products carries standard **Warnings and Precautions** (not boxed warnings), including:

- 
Monitor blood pressure and sodium/potassium serum levels. There is increased risk of GI perforation in patients with certain GI disorders.

- 
Ophthalmic effects may include cataracts, infections, and glaucoma. Use in pregnancy carries risk, as fetal harm can occur with first trimester use.

- 
Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, and hyperglycemia are potential risks. Corticosteroids can produce reversible HPA axis suppression with the potential for glucocorticoid insufficiency after withdrawal of treatment.


📄 **Source:** [FDA Prescribing Information – Orapred ODT (Prednisolone)](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2010/021959s004lbl.pdf)

---

### 3. ⚠️ Recent Manufacturing/Quality Recalls (Not Safety-Based Withdrawals)

While prednisolone itself has never been withdrawn for safety reasons, **specific batches** of prednisolone-containing products have been recalled due to manufacturing quality issues:

#### a) Lupin Pharmaceuticals (2026) – Prednisolone Acetate Eye Drops

Lupin Pharmaceuticals Inc. voluntarily recalled 2,530,182 bottles of prednisolone acetate ophthalmic suspension USP, 1%, after the presence of a **foreign substance** was identified in certain lots, according to an FDA enforcement report.



The FDA classified the action as a **Class II recall**, meaning use of the affected product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, while the risk of serious health effects is considered remote.


📄 **Source:** [Fox Business – Prednisolone Eye Drop Recall](https://www.foxbusiness.com/lifestyle/millions-prescription-eye-drops-recalled-nationwide-over-contamination-concerns) | [Eyes On Eyecare – Recall Details](https://glance.eyesoneyecare.com/stories/2026-07-09/fda-initiates-nationwide-recall-of-2-5m-prednisolone-acetate-eye-drops/)

#### b) AbbVie / Allergan (2026) – PRED MILD Eye Drops

A recall of 2,736 bottles of a prednisolone-based steroid eye drop (PRED MILD, 0.12%, 10 mL) was initiated due to **failed stability specifications**, which could affect the drug's effectiveness and shelf life.



The PRED MILD recall was classified as a **Class III recall** (the least serious category).


📄 **Source:** [MedShadow Foundation – FDA Recalls and Warnings](https://medshadow.org/drug-updates-recalls/fda-recalls-and-warnings/foreign-substance-prednisolone-bottles-seizure-drug-mix-up/)

#### c) Promise Pharmacy – Prednisolone/Gatifloxacin Ophthalmic Solution

Promise Pharmacy voluntarily recalled one lot of Prednisolone and Gatifloxacin Ophthalmic Solution 1%/0.5% sterile, 3ml vials. The product was found to have unidentified small particulate floating in the solution.



To date, Promise Pharmacy had not received any reports of adverse events related to this recall. Potential adverse health consequences ranged from limited eye irritation and inflammation to permanent ocular damage.

Here is a target-focused answer that treats **NR3C1** specifically, and does **not** substitute the usual glucocorticoid-agonist annotation for the question you asked.

## 1. Disease mechanism in multiple myeloma; is NR3C1 deficient or overactive?

**Core disease defect in multiple myeloma (MM):**  
MM is fundamentally a **clonal malignancy of plasma cells** characterized by uncontrolled expansion of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow, driven by heterogeneous genetic lesions and support from the bone-marrow microenvironment. This leads to excess monoclonal immunoglobulin production, bone destruction, and progressive organ damage. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4806534/?utm_source=openai))

**What about NR3C1 in MM?**  
For **NR3C1** specifically, the disease-relevant pattern is best described as **reduced function / deficiency in the context of glucocorticoid response**, not overactivity. In MM and other lymphoid malignancies, **adequate GR/NR3C1 expression is required for glucocorticoid-induced apoptosis**, and glucocorticoid resistance has been associated with **downregulation/loss of GR expression**, impaired transcription elongation of **NR3C1**, and sometimes NR3C1 abnormalities in relapsed/refractory disease. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8992511/?utm_source=openai))

**Conclusion for Q1:**  
- **Disease-level mechanism:** malignant plasma-cell overgrowth in bone marrow. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4806534/?utm_source=openai))  
- **NR3C1 direction in the disease context:** **DEFICIENT / reduced functional signaling**, because MM cells’ steroid sensitivity depends on NR3C1, and resistance is linked to reduced NR3C1 expression/function rather than pathogenic NR3C1 hyperactivity. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8992511/?utm_source=openai))

## 2. Would direct NR3C1 inhibition by prednisolone correct or worsen that defect?

Given your stipulated framing that **prednisolone shows IC50/Ki binding activity against NR3C1 and therefore should be treated here as an NR3C1 inhibitor**, the **direct effect on NR3C1 itself** would be expected to **worsen**, not correct, the MM-associated NR3C1 defect.

Why? Because the relevant disease-linked issue for NR3C1 is that **MM cells need functional NR3C1/GR to undergo glucocorticoid-triggered apoptosis**, and reduced NR3C1 expression/function is associated with resistance. Therefore, a drug action that **inhibits NR3C1 directly** would move signaling in the same direction as the disease-associated deficit rather than compensating for it. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4256227/?utm_source=openai))

**Answer to Q2:**  
- **Direct NR3C1 inhibition would be predicted to WORSEN the NR3C1-specific defect**, because MM steroid sensitivity depends on intact NR3C1 function, and inhibition would further suppress that axis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8992511/?utm_source=openai))

## 3. Clinical use anchor: is prednisolone or a related compound used for MM or NR3C1 dysfunction, and what is the confirmed mechanism?

**Yes.** Prednisolone/prednisone and especially the closely related glucocorticoid **dexamethasone** are well-established components of MM therapy. FDA review documents explicitly note that dexamethasone has been used routinely in MM for decades and that its **anti-myeloma effect is mediated via the glucocorticoid receptor (GR/NR3C1)**. MM cell-line data also support that glucocorticoids kill **NR3C1-positive** myeloma cells but not GR-deficient resistant counterparts. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211379Orig1s000MedR.pdf?utm_source=openai))

There are also FDA-reviewed MM regimens containing **prednisone** as a glucocorticoid backbone component, confirming class-level clinical use in MM. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2022/761145s012lbl.pdf?utm_source=openai))

For diseases caused by **NR3C1 dysfunction**, glucocorticoid resistance syndromes are conceptually linked to abnormal NR3C1 signaling, but the clear clinical anchor here is MM: the validated therapeutic mechanism is **NR3C1 agonism/activation**, not inhibition. FDA and pharmacology reviews describe prednisone/prednisolone-class drugs as binding the glucocorticoid receptor and altering gene transcription through the receptor. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2012/202020Orig1s000MedR.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**So the confirmed clinical mechanism through NR3C1 is:**  
- **Agonist activation of glucocorticoid receptor (NR3C1/GR)**  
- leading to transcriptional programs that can induce apoptosis in susceptible myeloma cells. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211379Orig1s000MedR.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## Bottom line

1. **MM pathophysiology:** clonal malignant plasma-cell expansion in bone marrow. For **NR3C1**, the disease-relevant direction is **reduced/lost functional signaling**, especially in glucocorticoid-resistant MM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4806534/?utm_source=openai))  
2. If you treat prednisolone’s action on **NR3C1** as **inhibitory** based solely on the ChEMBL IC50/Ki binding interpretation, that **direct NR3C1 inhibition would worsen** the NR3C1-related defect in MM rather than correct it. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8992511/?utm_source=openai))  
3. Clinically, **prednisone/prednisolone-class glucocorticoids and dexamethasone are used in MM**, but the validated mechanism is the opposite direction: **NR3C1 agonism/activation**, which supports anti-myeloma activity. ([accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2019/211379Orig1s000MedR.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## 🔲 1. Black Box Warning (United States – FDA)

**Yes**, liothyronine carries an FDA **Boxed Warning** (commonly referred to as a "black box warning"). 
The Boxed Warning on liothyronine sodium states: thyroid hormones, including liothyronine sodium, either alone or with other therapeutic agents, should not be used for the treatment of obesity or for weight loss. In euthyroid patients, doses within the range of daily hormonal requirements are ineffective for weight reduction. Larger doses may produce serious or even life-threatening manifestations of toxicity, particularly when given in association with sympathomimetic amines such as those used for their anorectic effects.


This warning appears across all FDA-approved labeling for liothyronine sodium products.

📎 Source: [FDA DailyMed / FDA.report Label for Liothyronine Sodium](https://fda.report/DailyMed/57744c7c-af44-4bc4-a5a8-79f05710f469)
📎 Source: [FDA Label (NCTR-CRS)](https://nctr-crs.fda.gov/fdalabel/services/spl/set-ids/115a84c2-0126-4dd7-816e-1873875f1e49/spl-doc?hl=liothyronine)

---

## 🔲 2. Lot/Manufacturer-Specific Recalls (NOT Full Market Withdrawal for Safety of the Drug Itself)

Liothyronine has **not** been withdrawn from the market globally due to safety concerns about the drug itself. However, there have been several **manufacturer-specific voluntary recalls** of combination products containing liothyronine, due to manufacturing quality issues:

### a) Westminster Pharmaceuticals Recall (Risk of Adulteration)

Westminster Pharmaceuticals, LLC voluntarily recalled all lots, within expiry, of Levothyroxine and Liothyronine (Thyroid Tablets, USP) 15 mg, 30 mg, 60 mg, 90 mg, & 120 mg to the wholesale level. These products were recalled as a precaution because they were manufactured using active pharmaceutical ingredients sourced prior to the FDA's Import Alert of Sichuan Friendly Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., which as a result of a 2017 inspection were found to have deficiencies with Current Good Manufacturing Practices (cGMP). Substandard cGMP practices could represent the possibility of risk being introduced into the manufacturing process.
 
This recall has since been completed and the FDA has terminated it.


📎 Source: [FDA – Westminster Pharmaceuticals Recall](https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts/westminster-pharmaceuticals-llc-issues-voluntary-nationwide-recall-levothyroxine-and-liothyronine)

### b) Acella Pharmaceuticals (NP Thyroid® – Sub-Potency)

Acella Pharmaceuticals recalled certain lots of NP Thyroid® because routine testing found them to be sub-potent — containing less than 90% of the labeled amount of liothyronine (T3) and/or levothyroxine (T4). NP Thyroid® is composed of levothyroxine and liothyronine, and is used to treat hypothyroidism.


📎 Source: [FDA – Acella Pharmaceuticals Recall](https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts/acella-pharmaceuticals-llc-issues-voluntary-nationwide-recall-certain-lots-np-thyroidr-thyroid-0)

### c) RLC Labs (Nature-Throid® and WP Thyroid® – Sub-Potency)

RLC Labs, Inc. voluntarily recalled a total of 483 lots of Nature-Throid® and WP Thyroid® in all strengths because FDA testing found the samples to be sub-potent. The product may have had as low as 87% of the labeled amount of Liothyronine (T3) or Levothyroxine (T4). These products are composed of liothyronine and levothyroxine and are used to treat hypothyroidism.


📎 Source: [FDA – RLC Labs Recall](https://www.fda.gov/safety/recalls-market-withdrawals-safety-alerts/rlc-labs-inc-issues-voluntary-nationwide-recall-all-lots-nature-throid-and-wp-thyroid-current)

---

## 🔲 3. No Global Safety-Based Market Withdrawal of Liothyronine Itself

Importantly, 
the Federal Register includes a determination that liothyronine sodium products were **not discontinued or withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons**.



Liothyronine was approved for medical use in 1956, is available as a generic medication, and in 2023, it was the 220th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 1 million prescriptions.


---

## 🔲 4. UK/NHS Prescribing Restrictions (Not a Safety Withdrawal, But Restricted Access)

In the United Kingdom, liothyronine has faced **prescribing restrictions** due to cost concerns, not direct safety issues. 
NHS England policy guidance recommends that liothyronine should only be initiated by an NHS consultant endocrinologist when being prescribed for the treatment of hypothyroidism, should be prescribed only if no alternative intervention or medicine is clinically appropriate or available for the patient, and patients taking liothyronine who have not already been reviewed should be reviewed by an NHS consultant endocrinologist.


This controversy was also tied to a pricing scandal: 
The British Competition and Markets Authority launched an investigation into the alleged "excessive and unfair pricing" of liothyronine tablets in 2017, alleging that Advanz Pharma overcharged the NHS from before 2007 to July 2017. The price of a pack increased by almost 1,600% from £4.46 before it was debranded in 2007 to £258.19 by July 2017.


📎 Source: [NHS England – Liothyronine Advice for Prescribers](https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/liothyronine-advice-for-prescribers/)
📎 Source: [Wikipedia – Liothyronine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liothyronine)

---

## 🔲 5. Safety Concerns from Compounding Errors and Misuse


Adverse events linked to liothyronine were mostly due to pharmacy compounding errors (10 cases) or the unlicensed use of LT3 for bodybuilding, weight loss, or fatigue in individuals without hypothyroidism (14 cases). Compounding errors involved the ingestion of LT3 doses that were 10 to 1,000 times the intended doses, equivalent to daily dose ranges of 1,000 to 50,000 mcg. Thyrotoxicosis, thyroid storm, or thyrotoxic periodic paralysis were the most frequently reported adverse events, and these usually resolved on discontinuing the offending preparation.



LT3-related adverse events were only reported with unregulated LT3 use or pharmacy compounding errors.

## Pazopanib (Votrient): Withdrawal, Black Box Warning, and Discontinuation History

---

### 1. ✅ Black Box Warning — YES

**Pazopanib does carry an FDA black box (boxed) warning**, which is the most serious warning the FDA can require on a drug label.


The VOTRIENT (pazopanib) label, present since the drug's initial U.S. approval in 2009, carries a **WARNING: HEPATOTOXICITY** boxed warning, noting that "severe and fatal hepatotoxicity has been observed in clinical studies" and that hepatic function must be monitored, with dosing interrupted, reduced, or discontinued as recommended.



A boxed warning about the risk of hepatotoxicity is included in the prescribing information for pazopanib, with severe or fatal hepatotoxicity manifested as increases in aminotransferases and bilirubin reported in patients receiving the drug.



Most (92%) cases of aminotransferase elevations of any grade occurred during the first 18 weeks of therapy. In the randomized, placebo-controlled study in renal cell carcinoma patients, increases in ALT concentrations exceeding 3 or 10 times the upper limit of normal were reported in approximately 18% or 4%, respectively, of patients receiving pazopanib.


📎 **Sources:**
- FDA label (2009): https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2009/022465lbl.pdf
- Oncology News Central monograph: https://www.oncologynewscentral.com/drugs/monograph/153214-310010/pazopanib-oral

---

### 2. ❌ Withdrawn from Market for Safety Reasons — NO


The FDA has formally determined that VOTRIENT (pazopanib hydrochloride) tablets, 400 milligrams, were **not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness**, and after independently evaluating relevant literature and data for possible postmarketing adverse events, the agency found no information that would indicate the drug was withdrawn for those reasons.



VOTRIENT (pazopanib hydrochloride) tablets, 400 mg, are currently listed in the "Discontinued Drug Product List" section of the Orange Book. A citizen petition was submitted requesting this determination, and after reviewing agency records, the FDA confirmed that Votrient was not withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness.



The Agency continues to list VOTRIENT in the "Discontinued Drug Product List" section of the Orange Book, which "delineates, among other items, drug products that have been discontinued from marketing for reasons *other than* safety or effectiveness."


In other words, the brand-name 400 mg tablet was discontinued from the market (likely for commercial/business reasons), but **not due to safety or efficacy concerns**.

📎 **Source:**
- Federal Register (August 5, 2021): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/08/05/2021-16692/determination-that-votrient-pazopanib-hydrochloride-tablets-400-milligrams-were-not-withdrawn-from

---

### 3. ⚠️ Discontinued for Safety Reasons in Combination Use — PARTIAL YES

While pazopanib **as a monotherapy** has not been discontinued for safety reasons, several **combination therapy trials were terminated early due to safety concerns**:


Pazopanib is not indicated for use in combination with other agents. Clinical trials of pazopanib in combination with pemetrexed and lapatinib were **terminated early due to increased toxicity and mortality**. The fatal toxicities observed included pulmonary hemorrhage, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and sudden death. A safe and effective combination dose has not been established with these regimens.


Additionally, regarding an ovarian cancer indication:


While pazopanib demonstrated initial therapeutic properties in patients with aggressive fibromatosis, ovarian, and non-small cell lung cancer, **plans to apply to the EMA for a variation to include advanced ovarian cancer have been withdrawn**, and a license will not be sought in any country.


📎 **Sources:**

---

## Vandetanib (Caprelsa) – Safety History

### ✅ NOT Withdrawn from the Market
Vandetanib has **not** been withdrawn from any market for safety reasons. 
The agent was first approved by the FDA in 2011 for the treatment of patients with medullary thyroid cancer with disease progression or whose disease cannot be removed surgically.
 
The European Commission granted a marketing authorisation valid throughout the European Union for Caprelsa on 17 February 2012.
 The drug remains available in both the U.S. and Europe to this day.

---

### ⚠️ YES – Black Box (Boxed) Warning Issued at Approval


The drug has been given a boxed warning that notes the risk of treatment-related QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, and sudden death in patients taking vandetanib.


Specifically, the FDA label states:

- 
Caprelsa can prolong the QT interval. Torsades de Pointes and sudden death have been reported in patients receiving Caprelsa. Caprelsa should not be used in patients with hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, or long QT syndrome.


- 
While considering the initial approval of vandetanib, the FDA publicly wrestled with questions about the drug's cardiac risk. Data from clinical trials suggested the drug could prolong the QT interval and lead to cases of torsades de pointes. The FDA convened a meeting of the Oncologic Drugs Advisory Committee (ODAC) in December 2010 to offer feedback on ways to use what seemed to be a promising cancer medicine safely.


**Source:** [FDA Prescribing Label (2011)](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2011/022405s001lbl.pdf)

---

### 🔒 YES – A Restricted Distribution (REMS) Program Was Required at Approval


Because of the risk of QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, and sudden death, Caprelsa was available only through a restricted distribution program called the Caprelsa REMS Program.
 
A REMS is a safety program that the FDA can require for certain medications with serious safety concerns to help ensure the benefits of the medication outweigh its risks. The safety requirements for Caprelsa included mandatory training for health care providers and monitoring of patients.


---

### ✅ REMS Program Removed in September 2025 (Due to Demonstrated Safety)


The U.S. Food and Drug Administration removed the Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS) program for Caprelsa (vandetanib), a thyroid cancer medication manufactured by Genzyme Corporation (now Sanofi).



After more than a decade of oversight, REMS assessments reported no cases of Torsades de Pointes or unexplained sudden deaths among U.S. patients taking Caprelsa. Clinical data also showed no concerning patterns of heart rhythm problems.



With the removal of the REMS program, vandetanib will continue to be available under its current prescribing information; however, oncologists will no longer be required to obtain special certification or follow additional REMS-specific monitoring requirements beyond routine clinical practice.


**Source:** [FDA Press Release – September 25, 2025](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-removes-risk-evaluation-and-mitigation-strategies-rems-caprelsa-vandetanib)

---

### ⚠️ Other Serious Warnings (Still in Prescribing Information)

Even without the REMS, vandetanib still carries several serious warnings in its prescribing information:

- 
Fatal skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and severe toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported; patients should permanently discontinue therapy for severe skin reactions; photosensitivity reactions can occur during treatment and up to 4 months after discontinuing.

- 
Interstitial lung disease (ILD), resulting in death, has been reported; therapy should be interrupted and unexplained dyspnea, cough, and fever investigated; vandetanib should be discontinued if ILD is confirmed.

- 
Heart failure has been observed, including some fatal cases; it may be necessary to discontinue vandetanib; heart failure may not be reversible.

- 
Vandetanib may cause fetal harm and is embryotoxic, fetotoxic, and teratogenic in animals.


**Source:** [RxList – Vandetanib Warnings](https://www.rxlist.com/vandetanib/generic-drug.htm) | [Drugs.com Monograph](https://www.drugs.com/monograph/vandetanib.html)

---

### Summary Table

| Safety Action | Status |
|---|---|
| Withdrawn from market | ❌ No |
| Black Box Warning (QT prolongation, TdP, sudden death) | ✅ Yes – since 2011 approval |
| REMS Restricted Distribution Program | ✅ Yes – required 2011–2025 |
| REMS Removed | ✅ Yes – September 25, 2025 (positive safety record) |
| Discontinued for safety reasons | ❌ No |

In summary, vandetanib has never been withdrawn from the market or discontinued for safety reasons, but it **does** carry a **black box warning** for serious cardiac risks that has been part of its label since initial approval in 2011. Its REMS program was lifted in 2025 as a result of more than a decade of post-marketing surveillance showing no cases of the most serious cardiac events.

## Miltefosine (Impavido): Safety Regulatory History

Miltefosine has **not** been fully withdrawn from any market for safety reasons and remains an approved, actively used drug. ### 1. ✅ Yes — FDA Black Box Warning (Embryo-Fetal Toxicity)


Miltefosine has a black box warning for embryo-fetal toxicity.
 This is the FDA's most serious warning category.

Specifically, 
IMPAVIDO (miltefosine) may cause fetal harm. Fetal death and teratogenicity occurred in animals administered miltefosine at doses lower than the recommended human dose. It must not be administered to pregnant women.



The FDA label explicitly advises use of effective contraception in females of reproductive potential, as noted in the Boxed Warning.



Miltefosine is contraindicated in pregnancy. Based on animal data, miltefosine may cause fetal harm. Pregnancy status must be verified prior to initiating miltefosine. To prevent pregnancy, females of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for 5 months after the last dose.


Additionally, 
miltefosine is listed as pregnancy category D by the FDA, meaning there is evidence-based adverse reaction data from investigational or marketing experience or studies in humans of harm to the human fetus.

Miltefosine was originally developed as an anti-cancer drug, but this development was halted due to unacceptable side effects.


Dose-limiting gastrointestinal adverse events in several phase I and II studies resulted in the discontinuation of the drug's development as an oral drug for the treatment of solid tumours. Its development as a topical formulation for treating cutaneous metastases of breast cancer continued though, and Miltex (Bayer, UK) has been marketed in Europe since 1992.

Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), sold under brand names including **Provera** (oral) and **Depo-Provera** (injectable), has a long and complex regulatory history involving **multiple black box warnings, early FDA rejections, and ongoing safety label updates**. While initially approved by the FDA in 1959 for treating conditions like irregular uterine bleeding, Depo-Provera's path to contraceptive approval involved **three major FDA rejections** in 1974, 1978, and 1983, with concerns ranging from potential cancer risks to ethical questions about clinical trials conducted primarily on vulnerable populations in developing countries without proper informed consent.



The primary reason for rejection was animal studies showing a link between medroxyprogesterone acetate and an increased risk of breast and endometrial cancers. Despite these concerns, Depo-Provera gained approval in several international markets, including France in 1969, and was widely promoted for population control efforts.

## 1) Disease mechanism

**Core pathophysiological defect in multiple myeloma (MM):**  
MM is a **malignancy of clonal plasma cells** that expand in the **bone marrow**, produce monoclonal immunoglobulin, and are sustained by intrinsic oncogenic lesions plus strong support from the bone-marrow microenvironment. A major disease feature is plasma-cell survival/proliferation with drug resistance, including resistance to glucocorticoid-induced apoptosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

**Is NR3C1 deficient or overactive in MM?**  
For the **NR3C1-specific axis**, the relevant abnormality in MM is best characterized as **functional deficiency / reduced NR3C1 activity**, especially in glucocorticoid-resistant or relapsed disease. Reviews and translational studies report that:
- glucocorticoids kill myeloma cells through the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by **NR3C1**;  
- **genetic anomalies/mutations in NR3C1** can block dexamethasone/prednisone’s pro-apoptotic effects;  
- **reduced NR3C1 mRNA/protein expression** is linked to glucocorticoid resistance and worse outcomes. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8992511/?utm_source=openai))

So the **primary molecular mechanism relevant to NR3C1 in MM is not receptor overactivation, but rather impaired/lost glucocorticoid-receptor function in resistant disease**, which prevents the normal GR-mediated apoptotic program in myeloma cells. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4693629/?utm_source=openai))

## 2) Target-specific direction for MEDROXYPROGESTERONE ACETATE on NR3C1

If we **accept your stipulated working assumption** that, for the **NR3C1 target specifically**, medroxyprogesterone acetate should be treated as an **NR3C1 inhibitor** on the basis of ChEMBL IC50/Ki assay activity, then its **direct action on NR3C1 would be expected to worsen, not correct, the MM defect**. That is because MM’s therapeutically relevant NR3C1 biology depends on **intact/active glucocorticoid receptor signaling** to trigger myeloma-cell apoptosis; reducing NR3C1 function would move in the opposite direction of the known beneficial GR axis in MM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

In short:

- **Disease-side NR3C1 state:** relatively **deficient / loss-of-function** in resistant MM. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8992511/?utm_source=openai))
- **Drug-side assumed NR3C1 action:** **inhibition**.  
- **Predicted target-direction match:** **mismatch** → would **worsen** the NR3C1 defect rather than compensate for it. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

**Important caveat:** outside your ChEMBL-based assumption, multiple primary/peer-reviewed sources describe MPA as a ligand with **glucocorticoid-receptor agonist/partial agonist activity**, not a confirmed clinical GR antagonist. Examples include studies showing that MPA binds GR and regulates GR-responsive genes, and immunology papers explicitly describing partial GR agonism. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10566649/?utm_source=openai))  
So the conclusion above is **conditional on your requested interpretation** of the ChEMBL NR3C1 binding data as inhibitory.

## 3) Clinical use anchor

**Is MPA or a close class relative an approved/investigational/experimentally validated treatment for MM or an NR3C1-dysfunction disease?**

### For multiple myeloma
I do **not** find evidence that **medroxyprogesterone acetate itself** is an approved or established investigational treatment for **multiple myeloma**. Current approved labeling for MPA is for gynecologic/contraceptive indications, not MM. ([dailymed.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=2627eb11-06bf-4a45-9172-094468e3ca07&utm_source=openai))

Resistance emerges when **NR3C1 is reduced or mutated**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

So the clinically anchored NR3C1 mechanism in MM is:

- **validated class:** glucocorticoids  
- **direction on NR3C1:** **agonism/activation**, not inhibition  
- **effect:** induction of myeloma-cell apoptosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

There are approved therapies for conditions involving glucocorticoid signaling, but the clinically validated mechanism is generally **GR agonism** with glucocorticoids, not MPA-as-NR3C1-inhibitor. Also, MPA itself is not an approved treatment for a canonical “NR3C1-deficiency disease” on the basis of restoring NR3C1 function. Its approved uses are primarily as a **progestin**. ([dailymed.nlm.nih.gov](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=2627eb11-06bf-4a45-9172-094468e3ca07&utm_source=openai))

## Bottom line

([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

2. **If MPA is treated as an NR3C1 inhibitor**, then its direct action on NR3C1 would **worsen** the MM-relevant defect, because MM benefits from **NR3C1 activation**, not inhibition. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10516567/?utm_source=openai))

3. **Clinical anchor:** MPA is **not an established MM treatment via NR3C1 inhibition**. ## Progesterone: Black Box Warnings, Market Withdrawals & Safety Actions

### ⚠️ 1. Black Box Warning Added (2002–2003) — Then Removed (2025–2026)


Hormone therapy use was highly common among women until 2002, when alarming results from the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) were released. A set of WHI trials suggested that varying forms of systemic hormone therapy that included **estrogen and progesterone** could increase the risks of cardiovascular problems, breast cancer, endometrial cancer, and possibly dementia.



Shortly after, the FDA implemented a **black box warning** — its strongest available measure short of removing a drug from the market — on all menopause treatments containing estrogen.
 This warning extended to progesterone-containing HRT products as a class.


The Prometrium (oral micronized progesterone) label received the same boxed warning despite the fact that the WHI did not study oral micronized progesterone. The warning stated that estrogens with progestins should not be used for the prevention of cardiovascular disease or dementia and should be prescribed at the lowest effective doses for the shortest duration.



The FDA required a further label revision in **2014**, incorporating updated safety language from the WHI Memory Study (WHIMS) data on dementia risk. The revision also strengthened warnings about the difference between progesterone and synthetic progestins, noting that results from the WHI study using medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) should not be assumed to apply identically to other progestogen formulations.



The black box warning led to a precipitous drop in hormone therapy use, from 27 percent in 1999 to just 5 percent in 2020.


**The Black Box Warning Was Subsequently Removed:**


After more than two decades of fear and misinformation surrounding hormone replacement therapy (HRT), the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) initiated the removal of broad "black box" warnings from HRT products for menopause.



This led to the **November 2025** decision where the US Department of Health and Human Services and the FDA announced the removal of the black box warnings, which went into effect in **February 2026**.



Boxed warnings were removed from **Prometrium** (progesterone, USP capsules), Divigel, Cenestin, Enjuvia, Estring, and Bijuva, spanning progestogen-only, systemic estrogen-only, topical vaginal estrogen, and combined systemic estrogen–progestogen products.



The agency worked with companies to update language in product labeling to remove references to risks of cardiovascular disease, breast cancer, and probable dementia.



It is notable that the higher risk attributed to the WHI study has been linked to **medroxyprogesterone acetate**, a formulation of progesterone "not in common use today for hormone therapy."


📎 **Source:** FDA Press Release — [HHS Advances Women's Health, Removes Misleading FDA Warnings on Hormone Replacement Therapy](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/hhs-advances-womens-health-removes-misleading-fda-warnings-hormone-replacement-therapy)
📎 **Source:** CancerNetwork — [FDA Removes Black Box Warning for Breast Cancer on HRT Products](https://www.cancernetwork.com/view/fda-removes-black-box-warning-for-breast-cancer-and-other-indications-on-hrt-products)
📎 **Source:** Harvard Health — [FDA Removes Menopause Hormone Therapy Black Box Warnings](https://www.health.harvard.edu/womens-health/fda-removes-menopause-hormone-therapy-black-box-warnings)

---

### 🚫 2. Progesterone Injection USP (50 mg/mL) — Listed as Discontinued, But NOT for Safety Reasons


Progesterone Injection, USP, 50 mg/mL is currently listed in the **"Discontinued Drug Product List"** section of the FDA's Orange Book. However, the FDA determined that this product **was NOT withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.**



This determination means that FDA will not begin procedures to withdraw approval of abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs) that refer to this drug product, and it will allow FDA to continue to approve ANDAs that refer to the product as long as they meet relevant legal and regulatory requirements.


📎 **Source:** Federal Register — [Determination That Progesterone Injection, USP, 50 mg/mL, Was Not Withdrawn From Sale for Reasons of Safety or Effectiveness](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/08/01/2023-16228/determination-that-progesterone-injection-usp-50-milligramsmilliliter-was-not-withdrawn-from-sale)

---

### 🚫 3. Makena (Hydroxyprogesterone Caproate / 17-OHPC) — Withdrawn from the U.S. Market

This is a **closely related synthetic progesterone derivative** worth noting for context. 
Makena's primary ingredient is a synthetic form of progesterone called **hydroxyprogesterone caproate** (intramuscular 17-OHPC).



The FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) proposed that Makena (hydroxyprogesterone caproate injection) be withdrawn from the market because the required postmarket study **failed to verify clinical benefit**, and the FDA concluded that the available evidence does not show Makena is effective for its approved use.



FDA withdrew approval of Makena and its generics because these drugs are no longer shown to be effective. FDA has withdrawn the approvals of Makena and its generics but recognized that a limited supply of these drugs had already been distributed.


📎 **Source:** FDA — [Makena (hydroxyprogesterone caproate injection) Information](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/postmarket-drug-safety-information-patients-and-providers/makena-hydroxyprogesterone-caproate-injection-information)

### 🚫 4. 17-Hydroxyprogesterone Caproate (17-OHPC) — Suspended in the EU


The European Medicines Agency's (EMA) safety committee (PRAC) recommended the **suspension of the marketing authorisations** for medicines containing 17-OHPC in the European Union. A review by the PRAC concluded that there is a possible but unconfirmed risk of cancer in people exposed to 17-OHPC in the womb. In addition, new studies showed that 17-OHPC is not effective in preventing premature birth.



Importantly, the EMA explicitly stated that **"the outcome of this review does not affect the use of progesterone,"** which works in a different way to 17-OHPC.

# Mifepristone: Market Withdrawals, Black Box Warnings, and Safety Actions

Mifepristone has a complex regulatory history that includes a **black box warning**, a **Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)**, a **brief voluntary withdrawal** in France, a **U.S. import ban**, and an **ongoing FDA safety review**. It has **never been fully withdrawn from any market for safety reasons**, but it has faced significant regulatory restrictions and political challenges around the world. Here is a detailed breakdown:

---

## 1. ✅ Black Box Warning (USA, since 2000)


When the FDA approved the chemical abortion drug regimen mifepristone and misoprostol in 2000, it recognized the dangers surrounding mifepristone and placed a **"black box warning"** on mifepristone's drug label — which is only used on the most dangerous drugs — about the risks of "serious and sometimes fatal infections or bleeding" that may occur.



The official FDA label for Mifeprex (mifepristone) tablets carries the boxed warning: **"WARNING: SERIOUS AND SOMETIMES FATAL INFECTIONS OR BLEEDING,"** noting that "serious and sometimes fatal infections and bleeding occur very rarely following spontaneous, surgical, and medical abortions, including following MIFEPREX use."


**The Black Box Warning was subsequently strengthened in 2004:**


The FDA announced it would revise the "black box" warning for Danco Laboratories' Mifeprex in response to numerous reports of infection, bleeding, and death among women who had taken the drug.
 
Although the drug's packaging already included a warning, the new warning was given "added prominence" and urged doctors to "redouble efforts" to monitor women for signs of systemic bacterial infections, excessive vaginal bleeding, and ectopic pregnancy.


📎 **Source:** [FDA Official Label – Mifeprex (mifepristone), accessdata.fda.gov](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2016/020687s020lbl.pdf)
📎 **Source:** [California Healthline – FDA Strengthens Warning on Mifepristone (2004)](https://californiahealthline.org/morning-breakout/fda-strengthens-warning-on-mifepristone/)

---

## 2. ⚠️ Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) — USA


The safety restrictions were codified as the **"Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy"** or **"REMS"** program, to ensure patient safety. A drug is placed on a REMS program when it is deemed "necessary to ensure that the benefits of the drug outweigh the risks," and REMS programs are designed to mitigate drug risks while still allowing patient access.



Mifepristone has a REMS classification — one of 73 drugs with such classification, a small fraction of the thousands of prescription medications approved by the FDA.



When the FDA approved the mifepristone-misoprostol regimen in 2000, it imposed restrictions in light of the risk of side effects such as heavy uterine bleeding. The drug had to be prescribed in person by doctors, and patients had to receive the drug in person and sign an agreement form acknowledging its risks.


The REMS has been **loosened over time**, not tightened:
- 
In 2016, the FDA expanded mifepristone to 10 weeks gestation and allowed non-physicians to dispense the drugs, reducing the in-person visit requirement to just one visit.

- 
With the latest REMS removal in 2023, in-person dispensing requirements were dropped completely.


📎 **Source:** [FDA Q&A on Mifepristone, fda.gov](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/postmarket-drug-safety-information-patients-and-providers/questions-and-answers-mifepristone-medical-termination-pregnancy-through-ten-weeks-gestation)
📎 **Source:** [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health – FDA Regulation of Mifepristone 2011–2023](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2026/study-fda-regulation-of-abortion-drug-mifepristone-from-2011-to-2023-shaped-by-evidence-and-caution)

---

## 3. 🇫🇷 Brief Voluntary Withdrawal in France (1988) — Due to Political Pressure, NOT Safety


Mifepristone was approved for use by French health authorities in September 1988, but opposition was so intense that less than a month later, Roussel-Uclaf said it would **pull the pill from the market**. Luckily the French government held a stake in the company, so the French health minister pressured the company to resume selling it.



Mifepristone was invented by a French drug company, Roussel-Uclaf, in 1980 and won approval in France in 1988. But the French company **suspended distribution** that year after threats from groups that oppose abortion rights. It lasted **two days** before the French health minister — noting that France owned part of the company — ordered it back on the market.


This withdrawal was **driven entirely by political and anti-abortion pressure**, not by any finding of medical safety concerns.

📎 **Source:** [France 24 – The Long and Winding History of the War on Abortion Drugs](https://www.france24.com/en/health/20230426-the-long-and-winding-history-of-the-war-on-abortion-drugs)
📎 **Source:** [NPR – Mifepristone's Status Is in Question: Here's How the FDA Handled Approving It](https://www.npr.org/sections/health-shots/2023/04/14/1169859888/abortion-drug-mifepristone-history-fda-approval-supreme-court)

---

## 4. 🇺🇸 U.S. Import Ban (1989) — Political, Not Safety


In the United States, the FDA **banned the importation of mifepristone in 1989**. The manufacturer of mifepristone, Roussel-Uclaf, also banned mifepristone distribution in the United States and refused to supply it to researchers investigating the drug's other possible health benefits.


This import ban was a political decision driven by anti-abortion pressure, not by safety findings. The drug was not approved for U.S. use until 2000.

📎 **Source:** [Reproductive Health Access Project – The History of Mifepristone](https://www.reproductiveaccess.org/2023/04/history-of-mifepristone/)

---

## 5. 🏛️ U.S. Court Challenges (2023–Present) — Attempted but Unsuccessful Judicial Withdrawal


In 2023, a U.S. District Judge in Texas (Matthew Kacsmaryk) attempted to **suspend the FDA's approval of mifepristone**.
 However, the case was ultimately decided by the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled the plaintiffs lacked standing, and mifepristone **remained on the market**.

📎 **Source:** [Feminist Majority Foundation – Mifepristone Timeline](https://feminist.org/our-work/mifepristone/timeline/)

Here is a comprehensive summary of the safety regulatory history of **Lapatinib (Tykerb/Tyverb)**:

---

## Lapatinib (Tykerb/Tyverb) — Safety Regulatory History

### ✅ Has It Been Withdrawn from Any Market?

**No.** Lapatinib has **not** been withdrawn from any market for safety or efficacy reasons. 
The drug currently has approval for sale and clinical use in the US, Australia, Bahrain, Kuwait, Venezuela, Brazil, New Zealand, South Korea, Switzerland, Japan, Jordan, the European Union, Lebanon, India, and Pakistan.
 It also does **not** appear on the U.S. FDA's official list of drugs withdrawn for safety or efficacy reasons (21 CFR 216.24), which enumerates substances that may not be compounded because they were found unsafe or ineffective.

---

### ⚠️ Black Box Warning — YES

**Lapatinib does carry an FDA Black Box Warning for hepatotoxicity.** This is the most serious type of warning the FDA can require.

- 
Tykerb (lapatinib) has a black box warning for hepatotoxicity. Hepatotoxicity has been observed in clinical trials and postmarketing experience. The hepatotoxicity may be severe and deaths have been reported. Causality of the deaths is uncertain.


- 
Lapatinib has been reported to cause severe liver damage within days to several months after the initiation of treatment, leading to a black box warning.


- 
The hepatotoxicity may occur days to several months after initiation of treatment. Liver function tests (transaminases, bilirubin, and alkaline phosphatase) should be monitored before initiation of treatment, every 4 to 6 weeks during treatment, and as clinically indicated.


- 
The association of the HLA-DQA1\*02:01 and HLA-DRB1\*07:01 alleles with hepatotoxicity in people who have taken lapatinib was mentioned in the FDA-approved drug label for lapatinib. The Swiss drug label for lapatinib (Tyverb) cautions for increased risk of drug-induced liver injury in carriers of these HLA alleles.


📌 **Source:** FDA Label (Tykerb): [https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2010/022059s3s6lbl.pdf](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2010/022059s3s6lbl.pdf)
📌 **Source:** Global Reach Health: [https://www.globalreachhealth.com/tykerb-generic-launched/](https://www.globalreachhealth.com/tykerb-generic-launched/)
📌 **Source:** Oxford Academic / Toxicological Sciences: [https://academic.oup.com/toxsci/article/197/1/69/7288208](https://academic.oup.com/toxsci/article/197/1/69/7288208)

---

### 🚨 Other Serious Safety Warnings (Warnings & Precautions)

Although not part of the Black Box Warning, the FDA prescribing label includes several other serious warnings that can lead to permanent discontinuation:

1. **Decreased Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (LVEF) / Cardiac Events:**

Lapatinib tablets should be discontinued in patients with a decreased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) that is Grade 2 or greater by NCI CTCAE v3.0, and in patients with an LVEF that drops below the institution's lower limit of normal.


2. **Interstitial Lung Disease / Pneumonitis:**

Lapatinib has been associated with interstitial lung disease and pneumonitis. Lapatinib tablets should be discontinued if patients experience severe pulmonary symptoms.


3. **QT Prolongation:**

Lapatinib may prolong the QT interval in some patients. Electrocardiogram (ECG) and electrolyte monitoring should be considered.


4. **Severe Diarrhea:**

Lapatinib should be permanently discontinued in patients with diarrhea which is NCI CTCAE Grade 4.


5. **Severe Cutaneous Reactions:**

If life-threatening reactions such as erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or toxic epidermal necrolysis are suspected, treatment with lapatinib should be discontinued.


6. **Fetal Toxicity:**

In animal reproductive studies, administration of lapatinib to pregnant rats during the period of organogenesis and through lactation led to death of offspring within the first 4 days after birth. When administered to pregnant animals during the period of organogenesis, lapatinib caused fetal anomalies (rats) or abortions (rabbits) at maternally toxic doses.


📌 **Source:** DailyMed (NIH): [https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=50d0dd0c-7682-43d0-aa1b-ca26e9181aee](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=50d0dd0c-7682-43d0-aa1b-ca26e9181aee)
📌 **Source:** Novartis Prescribing Information: [https://www.novartis.com/us-en/sites/novartis_us/files/tykerb.pdf](https://www.novartis.com/us-en/sites/novartis_us/files/tykerb.pdf)
📌 **Source:** FDA Label (2017): [https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/022059s022lbl.pdf](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2017/022059s022lbl.pdf)

---

### ❌ Discontinued for Safety Reasons?

**No** — Lapatinib has **not** been globally discontinued for safety reasons. 
Most concerning events include diarrhea, hepatotoxicity (black box warning), decreased left ventricular ejection fraction, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis, QT prolongation, severe cutaneous reactions (erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis), hypersensitivity reactions, and fetal toxicity
 — but these have been managed through labeling, monitoring, and dose modifications rather than full market withdrawal.

Here is a comprehensive, well-cited overview of amiodarone's safety history, including its black box warnings, notable FDA safety alerts, and the story behind its brand-name discontinuation:

---

## Amiodarone (Cordarone / Pacerone): Safety Warnings, Black Box Status & Discontinuation History

### ✅ Still on the Market — But with Serious Warnings
Amiodarone has **not** been fully withdrawn from any major market for safety reasons. It remains an FDA-approved drug. However, it carries **one of the most extensive safety warning profiles of any cardiac drug on the market.**

---

### 🔲 FDA Black Box Warnings


Amiodarone (Cordarone, Pacerone) carries a **Black Box Warning** that it may cause potentially fatal toxicities, including **pulmonary toxicity, hepatic injury, and worsened arrhythmia.**



The FDA has mandated that the drug include a black box warning about **pulmonary toxicity and swelling in the lungs**, a problem that can affect up to 17% of people given amiodarone. According to the FDA, up to 10% of these cases are fatal.



The FDA warns that amiodarone injections or tablets be used **only for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias** or rapid heartbeats and should only be started in a clinical setting capable of heart resuscitation. The warning also points out that amiodarone could cause serious and potentially fatal lung problems, damage the liver, and worsen heart rhythm problems.



There are **two black-box warnings** concerning the possible risk of amiodarone causing sudden death and other life-threatening side effects, including an irregular heartbeat, inflammation of the lungs, and liver inflammation or damage.


**Source:** [drugs.com – Amiodarone Prescribing Information](https://www.drugs.com/pro/amiodarone.html) | [ACC – Amiodarone Considerations for Use](https://www.acc.org/~/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Tools%20and%20Practice%20Support/Quality%20and%20Clinical%20Toolkits/AFib%20Toolkit/Amiodarone.pdf)

---

### ⚠️ FDA Safety Alert (2005)


In **2005**, the FDA issued a safety alert warning patients and medical professionals that amiodarone may cause side effects like **pulmonary toxicity, hepatic injury, and worsened arrhythmia.**


**Source:** [Consumer Alert Now – Amiodarone](https://www.consumeralertnow.com/dangerous-drugs/amiodarone)

---

### ⚠️ FDA Drug Safety Communication (2015) — Amiodarone + Sofosbuvir Interaction


On **March 24, 2015**, the U.S. FDA issued a safety announcement of **serious slowing of the heart rate** when the class III antiarrhythmic drug amiodarone was used with hepatitis C treatment containing sofosbuvir in combination with another direct-acting antiviral (DAA).



This safety update was made based on the report of **nine severe cases of symptomatic bradycardia (slow heart rate) and one fatal cardiac arrest** in individuals caused by the amiodarone and Harvoni or amiodarone and Sovaldi plus another DAA combination.



The FDA announced changes in the labeling of the hepatitis C drugs **Sovaldi (sofosbuvir)** and **Harvoni (sofosbuvir/ledipasvir)** to warn about a risk of serious and potentially fatal bradycardia when either drug is taken with amiodarone.



The new labels warn that **sofosbuvir and amiodarone should not be taken concurrently.** If concomitant use is necessary, cardiac monitoring in an inpatient setting is recommended for the first 48 hours, and daily monitoring of heart rate should continue for at least the first 2 weeks of treatment.


**Source:** [The Medical Letter – Severe Bradycardia with Sofosbuvir and Amiodarone](https://secure.medicalletter.org/TML-article-1466c) | [Hepatitis News Today](https://hepatitisnewstoday.com/2015/03/26/fda-warns-about-cardiac-risks-associated-with-hcv-drug-combination-amiodarone-and-sofosbuvir/)

---

### 🛑 Brand-Name Discontinuation (Cordarone, 2017) — NOT for Safety Reasons


In **February 2017**, Pfizer, Inc. notified the FDA that **CORDARONE (amiodarone hydrochloride) tablets, 200 mg, were being discontinued**, and FDA moved the drug product to the "Discontinued Drug Product List" section of the Orange Book.


However — and this is critical — 
after considering a citizen petition and reviewing agency records, **the FDA determined that CORDARONE was NOT withdrawn for reasons of safety or effectiveness.**



This determination means that FDA will not begin procedures to withdraw approval of abbreviated new drug applications (ANDAs) that refer to this drug product, and it will continue to approve ANDAs that refer to the product as long as they meet relevant legal and regulatory requirements.
 In other words, **generic amiodarone remains fully available and approved.**

**Source:** [Federal Register – Determination That CORDARONE Was Not Withdrawn From Sale for Reasons of Safety or Effectiveness](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2017/08/16/2017-17302/determination-that-cordarone-amiodarone-hydrochloride-tablets-200-milligrams-were-not-withdrawn-from)

---

### 📋 Summary of Key Side Effects Driving Clinical Discontinuation


The most common reactions (>1%) leading to discontinuation of amiodarone hydrochloride tablets include **pulmonary toxicity, paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia, congestive heart failure, and elevation of liver enzymes.**



Amiodarone also has serious and life-threatening side effects that **can occur months after the drug has been stopped.**


---
